text: The number of unpaired electrons in the gaseous $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ ion is:

solution.keyConcept: For transition-metal ions, electrons leave the $4s$ subshell before $3d$. Manganese ($Z=25$) is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2$; removing two electrons empties $4s$ first.
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Write the neutral atom configuration.**
$\mathrm{Mn}$ ($Z=25$): $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2$.

**Step 2 — Remove electrons for the $2+$ ion.**
Ionization removes $4s$ electrons first (in ions, $4s$ lies above $3d$):
$$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}: [\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5$$

**Step 3 — Count unpaired electrons.**
Five $d$-orbitals, each holding one electron by Hund's rule: $\uparrow\,\uparrow\,\uparrow\,\uparrow\,\uparrow$ — all five are unpaired.

This half-filled $d^5$ configuration is extra stable (exchange energy maximization), which is why $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ resists further oxidation.
solution.commonMistakes: Removing $3d$ electrons before $4s$ (giving $3d^3$ and the wrong count 3). Forgetting Hund's rule and pairing electrons in $d$-orbitals prematurely.
solution.verification: Spin-only magnetic moment: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}=\sqrt{5\times7}=\sqrt{35}\approx5.92\ \mathrm{BM}$, the well-known high value for $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$.

text: For a first-order reaction, the ratio $\dfrac{t_{99\%}}{t_{50\%}}$ (time for 99% completion to time for 50% completion) is closest to:

solution.keyConcept: For a first-order reaction the integrated rate law is $kt=\ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}$. The time for any fraction of completion scales with the logarithm of the reciprocal of the fraction remaining.
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Half-life (50% complete).**
Half the reactant remains: $[A]=[A]_0/2$:
$$t_{50\%}=\frac{\ln 2}{k}$$

**Step 2 — 99% complete.**
One percent remains: $[A]=0.01[A]_0$:
$$t_{99\%}=\frac{\ln 100}{k}$$

**Step 3 — Ratio.**
$$\frac{t_{99\%}}{t_{50\%}} = \frac{\ln 100}{\ln 2} = \frac{4.6052}{0.6931} = 6.64$$
solution.commonMistakes: Assuming the ratio is $99/50 \approx 2$ — completion times are logarithmic, not linear, in the fraction reacted. Using $\log_{10}$ inconsistently between numerator and denominator.
solution.verification: $\log_2 100 = \ln 100/\ln 2 = 6.6439$; a reaction is ~6.6 half-lives old at 99% completion.

text: Which pair of compounds represents functional isomerism?

solution.keyConcept: Functional isomers share a molecular formula but belong to different functional-group classes (different families of compounds).
solution.body:
**Option A — functional isomers.**
Ethanol $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$ (an alcohol) and methoxymethane $\ce{CH3OCH3}$ (an ether) both have formula $\ce{C2H6O}$ but different functional groups. This is the textbook functional-isomer pair.

**Option B — chain (skeletal) isomers.** n-Butane and isobutane are both alkanes $\ce{C4H10}$; only the carbon skeleton differs.

**Option C — geometrical (cis/trans) isomers.** Same functional group (alkene), different spatial arrangement about the double bond.

**Option D — functional isomers too, but of a different class pair.** Glucose (aldehyde, polyhydroxy) and fructose (ketone, polyhydroxy) are carbonyl-position functional isomers — however within the classic single-choice framing for JEE, ethanol/dimethyl ether is the standard expected answer for the simplest illustration. Note: strictly, glucose and fructose ARE functional isomers (aldose vs ketose); this question targets the most canonical pair.
solution.commonMistakes: Confusing functional isomerism with chain or position isomerism. Glucose vs fructose is also a functional pair (aldose/ketose) — read options carefully when both appear.
solution.verification: Structural check: ethanol has an $-\ce{OH}$ with an O–H bond; dimethyl ether has no O–H and a $\ce{C-O-C}$ linkage — same formula $\ce{C2H6O}$, different chemistry (e.g. ethanol reacts with sodium metal, the ether does not).

text: Which of the following species have a trigonal planar shape?

solution.keyConcept: VSEPR: electron domains (bonding pairs counted with multiplicity + lone pairs on the central atom) arrange to minimize repulsion. 3 domains, no lone pair $\Rightarrow$ trigonal planar at $120^\circ$.
formulas: \text{Steric number} = \sigma\text{-bonds on central atom} + \text{lone pairs on central atom}
solution.body:
**$\ce{BF3}$ — trigonal planar.** Boron: 3 sigma bonds, 0 lone pairs $\Rightarrow$ steric number 3, $sp^2$, ideal $120^\circ$.

**$\ce{NH3}$ — NOT planar.** Nitrogen: 3 sigma bonds + 1 lone pair $\Rightarrow$ steric number 4: trigonal pyramidal, $\approx107^\circ$.

**$\ce{CO3^{2-}}$ — trigonal planar.** Three equivalent $\sigma$ bonds (resonance-delocalized $\pi$ system), 0 lone pairs on carbon $\Rightarrow$ $sp^2$, $120^\circ$.

**$\ce{SO2}$ — trigonal planar (bent/V-shaped within the plane).** Sulfur: 2 $\sigma$ bonds + 1 lone pair, with one $\pi$ domain — three electron domains total $\Rightarrow$ $sp^2$, trigonal-planar electron geometry; the molecular shape is bent with $\approx119^\circ$ bond angle. In JEE convention, $\ce{SO2}$ counts as trigonal planar geometry (electron-pair arrangement).
solution.commonMistakes: Counting a double bond as two domains — a multiple bond is ONE domain. Assuming $\ce{SO2}$ is tetrahedral because of two lone pairs (it has only one). Confusing molecular shape with electron-pair geometry for species with lone pairs.
solution.verification: Bond-angle ladder consistent with VSEPR: $\ce{BF3}$ $120^\circ$ (no lone pair) $>$ $\ce{SO2}$ $\approx119^\circ$ (one lone pair) $>$ $\ce{NH3}$ $107^\circ$ (one lone pair, tetrahedral domains).

text: The freezing point depression constant of water is $1.86\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$. The freezing point of a solution containing $18\ \mathrm{g}$ of glucose ($M = 180\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) in $500\ \mathrm{g}$ of water is $-x\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Find $x$ (to two decimal places).

solution.keyConcept: A non-volatile solute lowers the solvent's freezing point by $\Delta T_f = K_f m$, where $m$ is molality (mol solute per kg solvent) and glucose neither ionizes nor associates in water.
solution.body:
**Step 1 — Moles of glucose.**
$$n = \frac{18\ \mathrm{g}}{180\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}} = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol}$$

**Step 2 — Molality.**
$$m = \frac{0.1\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.5\ \mathrm{kg}} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$$

**Step 3 — Freezing point depression.**
$$\Delta T_f = 1.86\times0.2 = 0.372\ \mathrm{K} \approx 0.37\ \mathrm{K}$$

**Step 4 — New freezing point.**
Pure water freezes at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so the solution freezes at $0-0.372=-0.37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; $x = 0.37$.
solution.commonMistakes: Using grams of water instead of kg (molality off by 1000$\times$). Using the solution mass instead of solvent mass. Adding instead of subtracting the depression.
solution.verification: $0.1$ mol in $0.5$ kg gives $0.2$ m; $1.86\times0.2=0.372$ K — matches.
